review:
I never thought I’d enjoy this game as much as I did. I picked it up two winter sales ago for very cheap, after all, I’m a big fan of the Guardians of the Galaxy trilogy, which is among my favorite Marvel movies, and the game was on sale, so why not? Like a good Steam consumer, I bought it on a heavy discount and completely forgot about it, lol. Recently, when I got Dune Awakening, I realized I didn’t have enough disk space to install it, so I started deleting some games. I checked which ones were taking up the most space, and this one was sitting at around 85 GB. Because of my love for the movies, I decided to give it a chance before uninstalling. Honestly, I thought I’d play it for a couple of hours at best, but the game kept pulling me back in.

Now, let’s be clear: this game is a very straightforward experience. It’s a linear single‑player game with decent combat, little to no exploration, and no difficulty . Don’t come in expecting a GOTY masterpiece , come in expecting a fun ride.

There aren’t 100 side quests, 100 dungeons, or 100 bosses. Exploration is very basic (think “instead of going right, go left , jump some boxes and find a room with some money”). You don’t need to grind or farm to reach max level, and you won’t die to a boss 1000 times. It’s just a direct, streamlined adventure. I do enjoy complex games with multiple endings, thousands of side objectives, and endless collectibles, but sometimes it’s nice to play something without worrying about sinking 250 hours into it. This is a 25‑hour adventure at most: follow the road, fight enemies, watch a cinematic, repeat. Fun stuff 

Combat isn’t super complex either. You play as Star‑Lord, but you fight alongside the Guardians. You can issue commands to them during combat each has three skills and one ultimate. You can chain their abilities together for combos, which feels cool even if it’s not groundbreaking. For example, telling Groot to immobilize enemies, then having Rocket throw a bomb, or asking Drax to launch enemies into the air so Gamora can slash them for maximum damage. Nothing revolutionary, but still fun.

What I Liked
Characters: All of them have personality, and the voice actors did a great job especially the Guardians. They feel very similar to their movie counterparts, and their banter, jokes, and stories make the game feel alive.

Cinematics: The game has a ton of cutscenes. Some people complain about it, but honestly, I liked them. I’d rather have a cinematic explain something than a random NPC standing around delivering exposition oe some random text.

Environment: I don’t remember the last game where I stopped to admire the scenery this much. There are some wild, beautiful visuals, and the camera often pans out to give you sweeping shots of the world. Really impressive stuff.

What I Didn’t Like
The exploration. Most of it boils down to jumping around or opening side rooms. Too often, you see an edge you think you can jump to, but there’s an invisible wall. Or you look down from a bridge and see boxes, thinking you can land on them, but nope, another invisible wall. Thankfully, falling into the void doesn’t kill you outright, just deals damage, but it was annoying.

I liked it, the combat is repetitive and space combat is just annoying/bad. 

But the story and writing, especially the humour - that's where the game shines. Good shit, yeah.

Guardian of the Galaxy was a pretty decent single player romp. I really liked the overall story. It definitely felt like a guardian of the galaxy adventure. Most of the characters were pretty entertaining and had their own type of humors. The combat was kind of repetitive and occasionally clunky with the huddle mechanics being more annoying than actually cool. The exploration aspect could use some work because the team literally berates you for going off the beaten path which got old really quick.

This game has a lot of banter. Sometimes too much. There are enough dialogue triggers in this game that you can easily trigger a set of dialogue only to cut it off with a different dialogue trigger so you’ll actually miss what the prior conversation was going to say. You’re not going to get a lot of quiet moments in this game. It actually started to wear on me a bit. Just be prepared for that.

Related to the dialogue, Rocket is probably going to get on your nerve for way too long. I’m not sure what they were thinking with his character arc but I promise that he does get better later on in the game and actually stop being a broken record playing the blame game and develop into a enjoyable character.

This game has a fair amount of funny and weird moments. Some of which you can trigger. If you see a prompt for it then go for it. I try to think of what Peter probably would do and just role played like that. It worked out pretty well.

Last thing: Turn of the ray tracing. The game looks great without it. It looks even better with it on but it has a problem with it getting stuck on a cutscene when it loads up a ray traced reflection. Just leave it off. You won’t miss it and the game does run much better.

If there was an option to leave a mixed review, that's what I would pic. I've enjoyed the story, missions, characters, dialogue and combat but there are two things about this game that irk me to the point where I would leave a mixed review - annoying bugs and awful flight mechanics. The game's easy if you're playing on the intended difficulty so if you've played games for a while, I would recommend setting a harder difficulty. I've seen some people mention that this game has "puzzles" in levels but I wouldn't really call them that. They're more like hidden areas. [u]If you're looking for a game to gift someone who is new to gaming, this game's perfect.[/u] This is the kind of game I imagine casual and console gamers to play. It's real easy to pick up.

The bug I keep encountering in the final chapters, is a bug where the game thinks I haven't killed all enemies yet, thus doesn't let me proceed past a mission point so I have to restart from last checkpoint. Thankfully, it's not a big deal because there's an autosave feature which saves the game often. It takes about 3-10 minutes to kill all the enemies again to proceed. Annoying but not a game-breaking bug.

Actually there's another thing that irritates me about this game. Sometimes the direction is horrible. Like for when you have to pull out cables. There's NO indicators which cables and where so you just go looking around and waste time. Some of the design decisions made in this game make me think they didn't even test the game with real users.

I picked up Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy on a steep sale, honestly just looking for a decent distraction before some other games came out, and I ended up completely loving it. It’s a huge shame it launched around the same time as the failed Marvel’s Avengers game, because that definitely turned a lot of people away. The story is fantastic, and the art direction and environmental storytelling are genuinely some of my favorites in any single-player game. What really holds the whole thing together is the constant banter between the Guardians which genuinely made me laugh at times

The combat is definitely the low point, though. You only play as Star-Lord, and using his guns feels like you're throwing rocks at enemies most of the time. You do get to control the other Guardians as "abilities," which is a cool system, but I really wish they gave you more moves to choose from. Thankfully, the boss fights are varied and fun enough to make up for it. I was also surprised that the game has semi-branching paths; your dialogue choices actually matter and can let you skip puzzles or make certain fights easier or harder. If you're even semi-interested, or just want to play through a really fun 18-20 hour sci-fi action movie, I highly recommend it.

The combat was relatively simple, but hard to get used to at first. It felt really nice that I could actually command drax, gamora, rocket and groot to use specific abilities on different enemies. I do wanna point out though that the highest difficulty was almost too hard to complete. I had to eventually crank down the damage dealt to me to very low and the damage that I did to very high while keeping the difficulty on max, due to the amount of enemies spawning towards the end of the game. It would also have been nice if groot would get his ultimate ability to heal earlier, instead of giving this ability towards the end.

What I also loved about the gameplay was the level desing. Everything was well thought out and extremely satisfying to explore. I especially love guardian's ship which was the coolest to walk through especially since you could see extactly where in space you are located. It really felt like I was floating in space and some levels in the game gave me the ability to control the ship and shoot at the enemy ships as well. That was super cool.

What I didn't like was the timed button presses where I had to press a certain button or move my mouse at a specific time mid cutscene without warning. It kinda reminded me of beyond 2 souls where you had to press specific keys mid cutscene. What also confused me is that you could also get fake end credits where you could finish the game without actually getting to the real ending of the game. Especially since it's not like they prompt me for a choice to make, but instead hope that you notice that you could actually interact with that specific cutscene without any visual cues given. But these were relatively minor annoyances and they only happen once or twice in the whole game.

Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy delivers a masterclass in comic book storytelling trapped inside a deeply frustrating gameplay loop. It succeeds brilliantly as a narrative experience but stumbles hard the moment you pull the trigger.

The Highs: Characters and Story

The narrative and character work are the game's undeniable strengths. The overarching story is exceptionally well-written, capturing the distinct voices and dysfunctional charm of the crew. The dynamic between the Guardians feels authentic and credible, paying massive respect to their comic book origins. The constant banter, quiet moments, and chaotic arguments are consistently great, carrying the weight of the experience and making the team feel truly alive.

The Lows: Gameplay and Mechanics

Unfortunately, the moment-to-moment gameplay is a bad joke that actively undermines the narrative momentum. The pacing suffers immediately with a remarkably slow start, artificially prolonged by tedious jumping puzzles that bore the player rather than challenge them.

Combat mechanics cross the line into complete implausibility. Star-Lord’s signature laser blasters feel severely underpowered, reducing encounters to tedious slogs where you must shoot a regular bad guy a million times before they finally drop. While the baseline movement system is okay, it ultimately feels clunky in practice. Most glaringly, the so-called legendary Guardian feels thoroughly inept during actual gunplay—a massive flaw for a game where shooting should take center stage and happen much more frequently.

The game forces you to endure a mechanically boring shooter to experience a brilliantly written comic adaptation. It is worth playing for the banter and the heart, provided you have the patience to tolerate its clumsy, bullet-sponge combat.

Picked this up for cheap about a year ago, yet still feel ripped off somehow.
After playing about halfway through the story last year, I bit the bullet to wrap up the campaign so I'd have an excuse to uninstall this. 

[h3]Boring Combat Loop[/h3]

Combat is generic, barely evolving from around the 25% mark. You spray with Star-Lord's blasters, dodging around as you wait for your teammates cooldowns to finish. Even on the harder difficulty mode, there's barely any challenge here. While they offer an extended list of settings to adjust several factors for combat, such as cooldown time, player damage, etc. , nothing can fix the weak-feeling combat loop and I can't be bothered to dig into a septic tank in hopes of finding a shiny rock. I was earning maximum rank on practically every encounter, which made fully upgrading well before the 75% of the story trivial. 

Upgrades are easily acquired and you'll still be collecting resources well after getting them all, which makes me believe that the developers didn't think most gamers would bother to explore any of the levels.

I'll make a special mention of the "Huddle" system, where you call a time-out, listen to your teammates, then pick the obvious correct dialogue choice to get a buff while a random 80s song from the soundtrack starts blaring. It's neat for the first few times, but quickly becomes a momentum killer. I would oftentimes just ignore the popup (or trigger it accidentally) since combat encounters would sometimes go quicker without using it. Of course, bullet-spongey enemies are thrown in to encourage you to use it.

[h3]Milquetoast story and atrocious dialogue[/h3]

Story is fine, it's a by-the-by Marvel movie premise, so fans of the movies will recognize the familar patterns. Overall, I'd say it's weaker that what Marvel studios cooked up, especially because the story feels so stretched to fit a 15-20 hour playthrough. Suprisingly, the game offers choices that impact the finale, which was a plus. Story cutscenes and transitionary levels interrupt too much for my liking, which I guess is standard for this sort of AAA game, but nothing within the story is worth putting up with this pacing.
 
For the few (and I mean very few) character moments that got a chuckle out of me, what really brings this down to a negative review, is the [b]dialogue[/b]. During combat, cutscenes, transitionary sections, puzzle rooms, everyone is talking NONSTOP. Combat will ususally have them repeat the same lines of dialogue within a single encounter. Any stopping within a puzzle room will have the characters joke around while you look for the obvious "switch" to continue on. I wouldn't mind if the dialogue was good, but it feels like for every actually clever line, it's buried under ten BS quips.  Anytime you're not beelining to the next objective, you'll be inundated with grating, "big chungus quirky" humour. So much so I found myself practically speedrunning through the game just so I wouldn't have to hear it.

[h2]Only if you're willing to put up with some garbage dialogue and boring combat, and only for BIG discounts[/h2]

**Visually Stunning, Narratively Exhausting: A Tragic Case of Wasted Potential**

**Score: 65 / 100 (Not Recommended on Steam)**

*Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy* is a game that breaks your heart. During the first two hours, it feels like an absolute masterpiece. The graphics are jaw-dropping, the environments are breathtaking, and the soundtrack is a glorious love letter to 80s rock. You can clearly see the immense soul, passion, and effort the development team poured into this project. They set the groundwork for what single-player Marvel games can achieve in the future. Unfortunately, despite these magnificent peak moments, the game brutally self-destructs under the weight of its own terrible artistic direction.

**The Gameplay: Wooden and Frustrating**
The combat becomes an absolute chore. Playing exclusively as Peter Quill feels deeply unrewarding. Armed with weak blasters that deal negligible damage, you spend fights acting like a glorified puppeteer issuing commands to your teammates rather than feeling like a legendary outlaw. The "Huddle" mechanic—a brilliant idea on paper—fails in execution: the dialogue choices rarely reflect what Quill actually says, and half the time your team simply misses the point, ruining what should have been an epic moment. Combined with clunky movement, repetitive encounter designs, and frustrating, unnecessary mini-games, the gameplay loop quickly turns into pure exhaustion.

**The Script: Non-Stop Noise and Protagonist Humiliation**
The writing suffers from severe "banter fatigue." The team talks continuously, shouting over critical story beats, lore explanations, and environmental cues. Instead of feeling like a tight-knit family, the crew comes across as an ungrateful group of bullies who mock Quill every five minutes—begging the question of why anyone would follow him in the first place. Characters like Rocket are stripped of their tactical intelligence and turned into insufferable, shielded brats who face zero consequences for mouthing off to cosmic entities.

**The Story: A Overstretched, Tacky Mess**
What started as a charming, grounded adventure about paying a fine and dealing with personal trauma escalates into a bloated, absurd cosmic apocalypse. The plot relies heavily on ludonarrative dissonance: after you spend 20 minutes defeating a legendary dragon like Fin Fang Foom, a cutscene immediately triggers where Lady Hellbender knocks out your entire super-powered team with two gentle slaps, stripping away any sense of player accomplishment. The story is artificially stretched with endless fake-outs—including a insufferable late-game sequence—turning the final arc into a frustrating, tacky ordeal that completely overstays its welcome.

**Final Verdict**
*Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy* is not a total failure; its technical achievements, visual direction, and audio design deserve high praise. However, a game should be measured by the quality of the time you spend with it, not the number of hours it forces you to endure. It ruins its own potential by trying to do too much, constantly falling into absurdity and disrespecting the player's time.

Worth picking up only at a **steep discount** (under €10-€15) to appreciate the visuals and audio, but impossible to recommend at full price.

Never a dull moment throughout the campaign

Production quality: Outstanding… just what you’d expect from an AAA game.

Story: Lore goodness and great character development. This is one of the game’s strong points (although the game seems to be strong in everything else, too). I think I spent a good portion of my playtime doing nothing, usually stopping my progress in-mission just to see if there was going to be a conversation between the team. Don’t take my word for it; here is what one Reddit user commented:

“I was not expecting the incredible amount of banter available on the ship. It was very immersive. Each character would yell across the room depending on where the other person was, with realistic audio effects. I was used to running out of dialogue after 1 or 2 conversations in Mass Effect, but GOTG keeps it going for a while before the next mission. In-mission banter is just as plentiful.”

Gameplay depth and variety: OK. Definitely not close to Devil May Cry level of depth, but the learning curve is high enough to keep you trying something new throughout the campaign. But that's it, after first playthrough, curve flattens. 

Achievements: Very doable. You can get all the achievements on your first playthrough if you’re thorough. I managed to get all the achievements on my own. But you have to work for them, especially for the outfits achievement. Some of the locations of the secrets are ingenious, but they’re not impossible to find.

And most importantly, the game is enjoyable and stays true to the characters. It really felt like Guardians of the Galaxy as we know it. The chaos of it all, the craziness, the constant bickering and banter between the characters, the humor—the game captures the essence of it. (Don’t get me started about that fridge! You can look up a Reddit thread on this; the comments are hilarious - https://www.reddit.com/r/PS5/comments/sipnd5/guardians_of_the_galaxys_unclosing_fridge_door/)

My only gripe is that the game is not stable with Ray Tracing. Absolutely unacceptable for a game with this level of caliber. I found this thread but I already finished the game. Maybe this will help https://www.reddit.com/r/PlayGOTG/comments/1usamte/raytracing_fix_for_pc_nvidia/

Overall, if you’re looking for a relatively new single-player AAA game to play casually, this is the game to go for. You won’t be disappointed.

Overall, this was a surprisingly fun game and definitely worth playing through if you're on the fence.

Ran this on a 9800x3D and a 5080 at 4k. Visually it looked fantastic, no real performance hiccups or graphical glitches to complain about but this was using high end hardware.

Now for the annoying stuff.  I had to restart the game at least 4 times because quest triggers just completely broke. Reloading the last save usually fixed it, but still annoying when you're just trying to get through a level.

The Huddle mechanic... ugh. It sucked. First couple times it was kinda neat, and when the 80s music landed right it was funny. Reminded me of that Simpsons scene where they're stuck in the car with "Sunshine, Lollipops and Rainbows" playing. But after a few times it became super repetitive and completely killed the momentum of the fight. Half the time the song choice didn't fit the vibe at all and just made the battle feel awkward and forced.

Also felt like they introduced a ton of cool mechanics once, used them for five minutes, and then forgot they existed for the rest of the campaign.

Some of the puzzles were pretty obscure too. If you weren't paying 100% attention you'd get stuck easily. I know that's partly on me, but I'm an old guy and I actually like a bit of "yellow paint" to point me in the right direction when I'm tired. A toggle setting in the menu for puzzle hints would've saved me some headache  so that your average user doesn't need to be bothered by it.

Combat was solid for the most part. Gunplay felt fluid and easy enough to handle. The squad skills were fine, maybe a bit forgettable, but the menu was easy to navigate. The workbench upgrades were cool early on, but searching for a bench got tedious fast, and I ended up with a pile of useless extra materials by the end. Same with the money mechanic. Seemed huge early on when you get to Knowhere, but completely irrelevant right after that.

Bottom line, if you like Marvel and story heavy action adventure games, give it a shot. Honestly, I enjoyed the story here WAY more than the last Guardians movie, which felt way too over the top and forced. This game nailed the balance of cheese, humor, and heart much better.
I had a solid time with this game, definitely worth a play!

The writing is easily one of its biggest strengths—every conversation, joke, and sarcastic exchange between the crew feels authentic and perfectly captures the personalities fans know and love.

The gameplay is surprisingly engaging as well. While you only directly control Star-Lord, coordinating abilities with the rest of the team creates satisfying combos and keeps combat exciting throughout most of the adventure.

That said, the game isn't without flaws. There are quite a few minor bugs scattered throughout the experience, and the overall length can feel a bit excessive. The pacing occasionally slows down with noticeable downtime between major story moments, which can make certain sections drag.

Even with those issues, Guardians of the Galaxy remains one of my favorite Marvel games. Its fantastic characters, sharp dialogue, and cinematic presentation make it an unforgettable experience that every Marvel fan should try.

Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy is just as the populous say, an unexpected banger. For those that do not know, this game is part of a deal between Square Enix and Marvel to release a batch of games under the Marvel Games brand. Unfortunately, it came out after the release of the notorious Avengers game which made many skip Guardians with the expectations that it would be of the same quality as Avengers. To be frank, I have not played the Avengers game myself and cannot really say how it compares with this game. About this game though, it got me [i] hooked [/i].

Plot: The plot being a space-opera adventure with a rag tag group of a found family is what the Guardians are all about. Of course, most would be familiar with the MCUs version of the characters but fans of the comics could also find a lot of inspiration from the source material in this game. In a nutshell, the developers really dove into the characters of this infamous group giving each character an arc that would be completed to make the group whole. Not only is the story of the game intriguing and heartwarming, the amount of collectibles with lore in the game truly show the care the developers put into this game and how much they appreciate the source material. The ending truly showed how much the characters have grown and bonded together [spoiler] with certain quirks like Drax calling Gamora and Rocket by their real names and Peter trusting Rocket with his cassette player. [/spoiler]

Gameplay: Probably the most divisive part of the game is the actual gameplay of the game. In my opinion, the decision to only control Star Lord was a good one. As not only does it make sense from a plot perspective but it works for the type of gameplay they were going for. Being only Peter did not mean you just had an effect on his actions because as Peter you are the leader of the group, you call all the shots. This is further reflected with the other part of the gameplay, a telltale-like choice system where your choices affect the missions entirely. As Peter, you made the decision for the members to coordinate their attack and in some instances could make a few interesting combinations of moves. However, this gameplay loop does get a bit repetitive which the dev must have realised because the combat sections were paced to not be back to back with simple puzzle segments in between but I do not think this was fully solved. Overall, the choices you make to further the plot as well as changing it entirely is the main strength of the game and is what kept bringing me back because I wanted to know what happens next and the character interactions were so much fun.

Extra: Speaking of the character interactions, the banter between the Guardians as you travel through each stage made the game feel so alive, in a weird pseudo-relationship way it made me feel like I was hanging out with a group of friends just goofing and gaffing together. And the stages are just so distinct from one another which is exactly what I would expect from a space adventure. I could write about a lot more like the use of the licensed music and some of the character designs but I expect not many have even bothered reading this far into the review.

In conclusion, an 8/10 game (Yes this may seem to be generous) that could have gotten higher if the gameplay loop was less repetitive. It is being carried by the plot and characters that many would possibly not relate as they may not be a fan of the group themselves which is fair. What's the point of buying a game that does not have good actual gameplay then? I’m not saying it's unplayable, it just needs a little something to really shake it up a bit. Something for a possible sequel, I hope. Until then, this game would most likely always be considered “the better game that Square made compared to Avengers.”

It's a great game. The story and characters carried the whole experience! The writing is genuinely funny at times, and the way the Guardians constantly bicker, joke, and talk about completely random stuff makes them feel so alive. It pulled me in fast; you actually end up caring about this dysfunctional space family.

There's also no shortage of big, jaw dropping Marvel moments, and it's cool seeing some characters we know from the movies shown in a completely different light . A refreshing take that keeps things from feeling like a rehash.

Visually it's gorgeous too... vibrant, colorful worlds paired with a banger soundtrack that hits at just the right moments. Between the humor, the banter, and the vibe, it just feels immersive from start to finish.

Only real downside: the combat gets a bit repetitive after a while. It's fun early on, but it doesn't evolve as much as the story does although it is kinda fun to try different combos with each character as there are quite a lot of options of abilities.

Overall, if you're in it for the characters and story (which, let's be honest, is the whole point of a Guardians game), it's absolutely worth playing!
